6:["$","div",null,{"className":"lg:col-span-8","children":[["$","header",null,{"className":"mb-12","children":[["$","h1",null,{"className":"font-serif font-light text-5xl md:text-6xl text-navy mb-4 prose-headings:text-navy  prose-h3:text-3xl prose-h3:mt-10 prose-h3:mb-4 prose-a:text-gold hover:prose-a:text-navy prose-a:transition-colors prose-img:rounded-md prose-img:shadow-md prose-img:mx-auto [&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Introduction and Colonial Caribbean Context"}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":["Sir Hans Sloane (1660–1753) was an Anglo-Irish physician, naturalist, polymath, and collector whose fifteen-month residency in Jamaica during the late seventeenth century profoundly transformed Western science, global culinary history, and museum institutions [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"1"}],"]. Operating during the turbulent zenith of the transatlantic plantation economy, Sloane arrived in the Caribbean when Port Royal was renowned worldwide as the \"Wickedest City on Earth\"—a bustling, cosmopolitan, and hedonistic privateer haven and slave-trading emporium perched precariously upon the sandy Palisadoes spit of Jamaica [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"2"}],"]. Though Sloane's sojourn on the island lasted only from December 1687 to March 1689, his methodical documentation of Jamaican flora, fauna, diseases, and seismic disasters laid the empirical groundwork for modern tropical medicine and botanical taxonomy [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]. Moreover, his personal encounters in Port Royal—ranging from his clinical treatment of the notorious privateer and former Lieutenant Governor ",["$","$Lb","a-3",{"slug":"henry-morgan","href":"/profiles/henry-morgan","children":"Capt. Henry Morgan"}]," to his compilation of survivor testimonies from the catastrophic 1692 earthquake—created the definitive scientific and historical record of seventeenth-century Jamaica [",["$","a","a-4",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"4"}],"]."]}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":["Beyond his scholarly contributions, Sloane's Caribbean career proved culturally and institutionally revolutionary. While in Jamaica, he observed local methods of preparing cocoa, refining the beverage by blending it with milk and sugar to produce the prototype for modern milk chocolate [","$Lc","]. Decades later, the vast fortune he acquired through marriage to a Jamaican sugar plantation heiress enabled him to assemble an unprecedented collection of over 71,000 artifacts, natural specimens, books, and manuscripts [","$Ld","]. Upon his death in 1753, this monumental Caribbean-derived collection was bequeathed to the British Crown, directly establishing the British Museum, the Natural History Museum, and the British Library [","$Le","]. Today, Dr. Hans Sloane stands as a towering yet complex Enlightenment figure whose intellectual legacy is inextricably linked to the natural wealth, human suffering, and ecological riches of colonial Jamaica."]}],"\n","$Lf","\n","$L10","\n","$L11","\n","$L12","\n","$L13","\n","$L14","\n","$L15","\n","$L16","\n","$L17","\n","$L18","\n","$L19","\n","$L1a","\n","$L1b","\n","$L1c","\n","$L1d","\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f","\n","$L20","\n","$L21","\n","$L22","\n","$L23","\n","$L24","\n","$L25","\n","$L26","\n","$L27","\n","$L28","\n","$L29","\n","$L2a","\n","$L2b","\n","$L2c","\n","$L2d","\n","$L2e"]}]]}],"$L2f","$L30",false]}],"$L31"]}]
7:["$","script","script-0",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/2uyb8-0enc77-.js","async":true}]
8:["$","script","script-1",{"src":"/_next/static/chunks/2z-jpqdx1wamk.js","async":true}]

a:["$","$L32",null,{"children":["$","$33",null,{"name":"Next.MetadataOutlet","children":"$@34"}]}]
c:["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"5"}]
d:["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"6"}]
e:["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"7"}]
f:["$","p","p-2",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/eb/Sir_Hans_Sloane_by_Stephen_Slaughter.jpg","alt":"Portrait of Sir Hans Sloane by Stephen Slaughter (1736)"}]}]
10:["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"Early Life, Scientific Training, and Voyage to the Caribbean"}]
11:["$","p","p-3",{"children":["Hans Sloane was born on April 16, 1660, in Killyleagh, County Down, in the north of Ireland [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"8"}],"]. He was the seventh son of Alexander Sloane, a Protestant receiver of taxes of Scottish descent who managed estates for the Hamilton family [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"8"}],"]. As a youth, Sloane exhibited an intense, instinctive fascination with the natural world, spending countless hours scouring the County Down countryside for unusual stones, insects, and botanical specimens [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"9"}],"]. At age sixteen, his academic ambitions were suddenly interrupted by a severe pulmonary hemorrhage (hemoptysis), which incapacitated him for three years [",["$","a","a-3",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"10"}],"]. This brush with mortality compelled Sloane to adopt a lifelong regimen of strict dietary temperance and piqued his interest in human anatomy, pharmacology, and clinical medicine [",["$","a","a-4",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"10"}],"]."]}]
12:["$","p","p-4",{"children":["Upon regaining his strength in 1679, Sloane moved to London to formally pursue medical and botanical studies. He trained under renowned apothecary John Ray, studied chemistry under Robert Boyle, and attended botanical lectures at the Chelsea Physic Garden [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"1"}],"]. Seeking the finest continental clinical instruction, Sloane traveled to France in 1683, attending medical lectures in Paris and Montpellier before graduating with his Doctor of Medicine degree from the University of Orange in July 1683 [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"9"}],"]. Returning to London with extensive botanical herbaria, he established a thriving medical practice and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1685 at the youthful age of twenty-four, followed by admission as a Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians in 1687 [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"8"}],"]."]}]
13:["$","p","p-5",{"children":["Despite his burgeoning success in London, Sloane harbored an ambition to explore the uncharted biodiversity of the New World. In 1687, fortune presented an extraordinary opportunity: Christopher Monck, the 2nd Duke of Albemarle, was appointed Governor of Jamaica by King James II and sought a personal physician to accompany his aristocratic household [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"2"}],"]. Sloane eagerly accepted the appointment at an annual salary of £600, viewing the tropical island as an untouched scientific frontier [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]. On September 12, 1687, Sloane embarked aboard the frigate ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"HMS Assistance"}],", sailing via Madeira, Barbados, Nevis, and St. Kitts before dropping anchor in the bustling harbor of Port Royal, Jamaica, on December 19, 1687 [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"1"}],"]."]}]
14:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"Port Royal Metropolis and Attending Capt. Henry Morgan"}]
15:["$","p","p-6",{"children":["When Dr. Hans Sloane stepped ashore at Port Royal, he entered the undisputed maritime capital of the seventeenth-century English Caribbean [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"2"}],"]. Squeezed onto a narrow, triangular sandspit that sheltered Kingston Harbour, Port Royal was one of the most densely populated and commercially vibrant cities in the Western Hemisphere, boasting four-story brick townhouses, bustling quays, fortifications, and lavish taverns catering to merchants, naval officers, buccaneers, and enslaved laborers [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"4"}],"]. As the Duke of Albemarle's chief physician, Sloane was immediately thrust into the medical and social epicenter of colonial life, treating high-ranking colonial officials, wealthy merchants, indentured servants, and enslaved Africans [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"2"}],"]."]}]
16:["$","p","p-7",{"children":["Among Sloane’s most famous patients in Port Royal was the legendary Welsh buccaneer and former Lieutenant Governor of Jamaica, ",["$","$Lb","a-0",{"slug":"henry-morgan","href":"/profiles/henry-morgan","children":"Capt. Henry Morgan"}]," [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"11"}],"]. In early 1688, the aging privateer was suffering from severe, debilitating health complications brought on by decades of tropical campaigns, heavy drinking, and extravagant nocturnal living [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"11"}],"]. Sloane conducted detailed clinical examinations of Morgan, recording one of the most remarkable medical case studies in Caribbean history. Sloane diagnosed Morgan with severe dropsy (edema) complicated by acute liver failure, describing the privateer as \"lean, sallow-coloured, his eyes a little yellowish and belly jutting out or prominent\" [",["$","a","a-3",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"11"}],"]. Sloane noted that Morgan suffered from persistent morning vomiting, chronic insomnia, and loss of appetite, and strongly advised him to abstain from alcohol and adopt a mild, temperate diet [",["$","a","a-4",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"11"}],"]."]}]
17:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":["\"He was lean, sallow-coloured, his eyes a little yellowish and belly jutting out or prominent... sitting up late and excessive drinking were the reasons of his indisposition.\" — Dr. Hans Sloane on treating Sir Henry Morgan, 1688 [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"11"}],"]"]}],"\n"]}]
18:["$","p","p-8",{"children":["Morgan, however, largely disregarded Sloane's advice, turning instead to local empirical healers and continuing to consume alcohol with fellow buccaneers [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"11"}],"]. Despite Sloane and local doctor Fulke Rose administering various contemporary preparations, Morgan's condition rapidly deteriorated. ",["$","$Lb","a-1",{"slug":"henry-morgan","href":"/profiles/henry-morgan","children":"Capt. Henry Morgan"}]," passed away on August 25, 1688, at his Lawrencefield estate and was laid to rest with full military honors in the Palisadoes cemetery outside Port Royal [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"11"}],"]. Sloane's clinical notes on Morgan, later published in his travel memoirs, provide an irreplaceable firsthand glimpse into the physical demise of the Golden Age of Buccaneering [",["$","a","a-3",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]."]}]
19:["$","p","p-9",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Port_Royal_earthquake_1692_by_Jan_Luyken_and_Pieter_van_der_Aa.jpg","alt":"Contemporary engraving of the catastrophic 1692 Port Royal earthquake by Jan Luyken"}]}]
1a:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"The 1692 Cataclysm and the Royal Society Earthquake Archive"}]
1b:["$","p","p-10",{"children":["Sloane's Caribbean residency was cut short by political and domestic calamity. In October 1688, barely ten months into his governorship, the Duke of Albemarle died suddenly in Jamaica following an extended bout of heavy drinking and fever [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"2"}],"]. Sloane performed the post-mortem embalming on the Duke's body, preserving it for transport back to England [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"8"}],"]. However, news arrived that the Glorious Revolution had ousted King James II, plunging England into political uncertainty and delaying the departure of the widowed Duchess of Albemarle until March 1689 [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"2"}],"]. When Sloane finally sailed for London aboard the ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"HMS Assistance"}],", he carried an extraordinary scientific cargo: over 800 dried plant specimens pressed into massive folio albums, preserved coral, live reptiles, and detailed notebooks recording Jamaican geography, climate, and society [",["$","a","a-3",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"1"}],"]."]}]
1c:["$","p","p-11",{"children":["Three years after Sloane's departure, a natural catastrophe eradicated the world he had so meticulously observed. On the morning of June 7, 1692, an earthquake with an estimated magnitude of 7.5 struck Port Royal [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"12"}],"]. Within minutes, the unconsolidated sandspit on which the city stood underwent catastrophic soil liquefaction [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"12"}],"]. Fort James and Fort Carlisle slid into the sea, entire streets of brick houses sank beneath the water, and an ensuing tsunami battered the harbor [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"4"}],"]. More than 2,000 residents died immediately, followed by thousands more who succumbed to malignant fevers in temporary refugee camps across the harbor at Passage Fort and the newly cleared site of Kingston [",["$","a","a-3",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"12"}],"]. Sir Henry Morgan’s tomb and cemetery were completely washed into the sea [",["$","a","a-4",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"11"}],"]."]}]
1d:["$","p","p-12",{"children":["Although Sloane was back in London, he played a central role in documenting this historical disaster for the global scientific community. Serving as Secretary of the Royal Society, Sloane used his Caribbean correspondence network to solicit, collect, and verify eyewitness reports and survivor testimonies from Port Royal [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"13"}],"]. In 1694, Sloane published these definitive accounts in Volume 18 of the Royal Society’s ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Philosophical Transactions"}],", under the title ",["$","em","em-1",{"children":"\"A Letter from Hans Sloane, M. D. and S. R. S. with Several Accounts of the Earthquakes in Peru October the 20th 1687. And at Jamaica, February 19th. 1687/8 and June the 7th. 1692\""}]," [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"13"}],"]. Through this publication, Sloane provided the Western world with its most authoritative, scientifically rigorous narrative of the destruction of Port Royal, making a foundational contribution to early modern seismology and geomorphology [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"13"}],"]."]}]
1e:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"Jamaican Cocoa and the Popularization of Milk Chocolate"}]
1f:["$","p","p-13",{"children":["Among Dr. Hans Sloane’s most famous Caribbean legacies was his transformation of drinking chocolate [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"5"}],"]. In seventeenth-century Jamaica, cocoa (",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Theobroma cacao"}],") was cultivated in plantation valleys, and cocoa beverages were consumed regularly by Spanish colonists, enslaved Africans, and Indigenous peoples [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"5"}],"]. When Sloane was introduced to the native preparation—a thick, bitter concoction made by boiling raw cocoa paste with hot water and local spices—he found it intensely disagreeable, writing that it tasted \"nauseous, and hard of digestion\" [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"5"}],"]."]}]
20:["$","p","p-14",{"children":["Recognizing the substantial nutritional value and stimulant properties of cocoa beans, Sloane conducted empirical culinary experiments during his time in Jamaica [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"14"}],"]. He discovered that by boiling ground cocoa paste with fresh milk and refined cane sugar, the astringent fats were emulsified, rendering the drink palatable, aromatic, and digestible [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"5"}],"]. Upon his return to London in 1689, Sloane introduced his milk chocolate recipe into his medical practice, prescribing it as a restorative tonic for patients suffering from tuberculosis, wasting diseases, and pediatric digestive complaints [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"14"}],"]."]}]
21:["$","blockquote","blockquote-1",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":["\"Chocolate was in use among the Native Americans, but the Spaniards and other Europeans added milk and sugar to temper its bitterness, rendering it both pleasant and wholesome to the stomach.\" — Dr. Hans Sloane, ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"A Voyage to the Islands"}]," [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]"]}],"\n"]}]
22:["$","p","p-15",{"children":["Throughout the eighteenth century, Sloane's formulation became immensely popular among the British aristocracy and urban middle classes. London apothecaries and coffeehouses eagerly marketed \"Sir Hans Sloane's Milk Chocolate\" as both a luxury beverage and an invigorating health elixir [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"14"}],"]. In the nineteenth century, the burgeoning chocolate manufacturing firm Cadbury Brothers acquired Sloane’s proprietary milk chocolate recipe, utilizing his esteemed medical name on their tins to promote their commercial cocoa powder [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"5"}],"]. Sloane's Caribbean experimentation thus served as the direct precursor to the global modern milk chocolate industry."]}]
23:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Ethnomusicology, Afro-Caribbean Medicine, and Enslavement"}]
24:["$","p","p-16",{"children":["Sloane’s Jamaica writings contain some of the earliest and most consequential anthropological observations of enslaved African communities in the Caribbean [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"15"}],"]. As a practicing physician visiting estates in Saint Catherine, Guanaboa, and the Liguanea Plain, Sloane closely observed the enslaved laborers whose forced labor powered the island's burgeoning sugar revolution [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]. While Sloane held the ethnocentric and racist prejudices typical of seventeenth-century European planters, his scientific commitment to empirical observation led him to record detailed cultural practices that were otherwise ignored by contemporary chroniclers [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"15"}],"]."]}]
25:["$","p","p-17",{"children":["Most significantly, Sloane published the earliest known musical transcriptions of African music in the Americas [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"16"}],"]. In Jamaica, Sloane observed musical gatherings where enslaved Koromanti, Angola, and Papaw laborers played handmade string instruments, rattles, and drums carved from hollowed logs [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"16"}],"]. Fascinated by the polyrhythmic complexity of the songs, Sloane enlisted a local European musician named Baptiste to transcribe the melodies and lyrics into standard Western musical notation [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"16"}],"]. These transcriptions, published in the introductory volume of his natural history in 1707, represent an indispensable historical archive of African musical retention and the birth of Afro-Caribbean musical genres [",["$","a","a-3",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"16"}],"]."]}]
26:["$","p","p-18",{"children":["Simultaneously, Sloane documented Jamaican ethnobotany and African traditional medicine [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"15"}],"]. He observed how enslaved healers used local wild plants—including ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Aristolochia odoratissima"}]," (contrayerva), wild sage, physic nut, and castor oil—to treat snakebites, intestinal parasites, and tropical ulcers [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]. However, Sloane's texts also starkly record the horrific brutalities of plantation discipline. In his memoirs, he matter-of-factly cataloged the gruesome punishments inflicted on enslaved runaways and rebels, including burning at the stake, castration, and suspension in chains, illustrating the violent foundations upon which colonial wealth and scientific inquiry were built [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"15"}],"]."]}]
27:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":[["$","em","em-0",{"children":"A Voyage to the Islands"}]," and Plantation Wealth"]}]
28:["$","p","p-19",{"children":["Upon returning to England, Sloane devoted decades to systematizing and publishing his Jamaican discoveries [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"1"}],"]. In 1696, he published ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"Catalogus plantarum quae in insula Jamaica sponte proveniunt"}],", a Latin botanical catalog classifying roughly 1,200 plant species, including more than 800 that were previously unknown to European science [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]. This was followed by his monumental two-volume masterwork: ",["$","em","em-1",{"children":"A Voyage to the Islands Madera, Barbados, Nieves, St. Christophers and Jamaica, with the Natural History of the Herbs and Trees, Four-footed Beasts, Fishes, Birds, Insects, Reptiles, etc. of the Last of those Islands"}]," (Volume 1 published in 1707; Volume 2 in 1725) [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]."]}]
29:["$","p","p-20",{"children":["Financed entirely by Sloane, ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"A Voyage to the Islands"}]," was an artistic and scientific tour de force. The work was illustrated with hundreds of intricate, full-page copperplate engravings executed by top European engravers, including Michael Burghers and John Savage [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]. These plates depicted Jamaican flora such as breadfruit, allspice (",["$","em","em-1",{"children":"Pimenta dioica"}],"), wild cinnamon, and mahogany, as well as fauna ranging from iguanas and manatees to hummingbirds and flying fish [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"3"}],"]. Sloane’s meticulous descriptions and taxonomic classifications directly informed Carl Linnaeus, who cited Sloane repeatedly in his revolutionary ",["$","em","em-2",{"children":"Species Plantarum"}]," (1753) and ",["$","em","em-3",{"children":"Systema Naturae"}]," [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"1"}],"]."]}]
2a:["$","p","p-21",{"children":["The immense wealth that allowed Sloane to publish these lavish volumes and assemble his collections was derived directly from Jamaican plantation slavery [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"6"}],"]. In 1695, Sloane married Elizabeth Langley Rose, the wealthy widow of Dr. Fulke Rose—the Jamaican physician and councilor who had collaborated with Sloane in treating ",["$","$Lb","a-1",{"slug":"henry-morgan","href":"/profiles/henry-morgan","children":"Capt. Henry Morgan"}]," [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"6"}],"]. Through this marriage, Sloane acquired a life interest in one-third of the income generated by vast Jamaican sugar plantations worked by hundreds of enslaved laborers, including the Guanaboa Vale estate [",["$","a","a-3",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"6"}],"]. This steady stream of Caribbean sugar wealth provided Sloane with financial independence, allowing him to purchase the Manor of Chelsea in 1712 and relentlessly purchase thousands of rare books, antique coins, manuscripts, and natural history cabinets [",["$","a","a-4",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"6"}],"]."]}]
2b:["$","h3","h3-7",{"children":"Later Presidency and the Foundation of the British Museum"}]
2c:["$","p","p-22",{"children":["In his later decades, Dr. Hans Sloane rose to the absolute summit of the British scientific and medical establishment [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"8"}],"]. In 1716, King George I created him a baronet, making Sloane the first British medical practitioner to receive a hereditary title of nobility [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"8"}],"]. In 1719, he was elected President of the Royal College of Physicians, a position he held with distinction until 1735 [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"8"}],"]. Most prestigiously, upon the death of Sir Isaac Newton in 1727, Sloane was elected President of the Royal Society, presiding over Britain's premier scientific academy for fourteen years until his retirement in 1741 [",["$","a","a-3",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"8"}],"]. In 1722, Sloane solidified his botanical legacy by granting the four-acre land of the Chelsea Physic Garden to the Worshipful Society of Apothecaries for a nominal perpetual lease, ensuring its survival as a center for botanical education [",["$","a","a-4",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"10"}],"]."]}]
2d:["$","p","p-23",{"children":["Sir Hans Sloane died peacefully at his Chelsea estate on January 11, 1753, at the age of ninety-two, and was buried at Chelsea Old Church [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"8"}],"]. By the time of his death, his personal collection was without parallel in the Western world, comprising 71,000 cataloged items, including 50,000 printed books, 3,566 bound manuscripts, 32,000 ancient coins and medals, 334 volumes of dried herbarium specimens, and thousands of ethnographical artifacts from the Caribbean, Africa, the Americas, and Asia [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"6"}],"]."]}]
2e:["$","p","p-24",{"children":["In his final will, Sloane bequeathed his entire collection to King George II and the British nation on the condition that Parliament pay £20,000 to his two surviving daughters—a fraction of the collection's estimated market value of £80,000 [",["$","a","a-0",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"7"}],"]. Parliament recognized the historic significance of the offer and passed the British Museum Act of 1753 [",["$","a","a-1",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"7"}],"]. Sloane’s Caribbean specimens, manuscripts, and antiquities formed the foundational core of the ",["$","strong","strong-0",{"children":"British Museum"}],", which opened its doors to the public at Montagu House in 1759 [",["$","a","a-2",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"7"}],"]. Over time, Sloane’s botanical herbaria and zoological specimens became the nucleus of the ",["$","strong","strong-1",{"children":"Natural History Museum"}],", while his colossal library created the foundation of the ",["$","strong","strong-2",{"children":"British Library"}]," [",["$","a","a-3",{"href":"#sources","className":"text-gold hover:underline","children":"7"}],"]. In modern times, global institutions have re-evaluated Sloane's monumentality, recognizing that the Enlightenment treasures of London were paid for and inspired by the natural richness, seismic tragedies, and enslaved laborers of colonial Jamaica."]}]
